summary: Defines naming and structuring guidelines for X.500 directory pilots, focused on white pages. Following them is recommended so pilots work together. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Rules for naming entries in a big phone book so every pilot project uses it the same way.

questions: what is a directory information tree
how should organisations be named in x.500
subtitle: How to lay out and name entries in an X.500 white pages directory so separate pilot projects fit together.

tldr.problem: Early X.500 directory pilots were each free to structure and name their data, which made searching across pilots awkward and inconsistent.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends a shallow, search-friendly tree under the standard country and organisation layout, full meaningful names with abbreviations kept as extra values, and specific uses for common attributes.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational set of guidelines for white pages pilots that obsoletes RFC 1384; it is advice, not a standard.

facts.value: A maximum of two should suffice

today: RFC 1617 is an Informational memo from May 1994 that obsoletes RFC 1384. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, according to the metadata for this page.

sections.title: Introduction and Audience
sections.content:
The guidelines are written for data managers who run X.500 Directory services. They help a manager decide how to model, for example, their organisation in the Directory Information Tree, and which data elements to store for each kind of entry.

The focus is the White Pages use of the Directory, the X.500 application with the most operational experience at the time. Many recommendations also apply to other uses. The document assumes the COSINE and Internet X.500 Schema from RFC 1274 is followed.
sections.eli5: This is a how-to guide for the people who keep a big online phone book. It helps them decide where each entry goes and what to write in it.

sections.title: Structure of the Directory Tree
sections.content:
Pilots should follow the structure suggested in Annex B of X.521, with a few restrictions. The top of the tree holds participating countries (named by ISO 3166 country code), international organisations, a few localities such as Europe, and a minimum of DSA information. International organisations, such as the United Nations, may be registered at the top. Multi-national commercial organisations may not.

Below a country come organisations of national significance, then locality entries for states or similar divisions. Large organisations may be split into organisational units, and people and roles are stored beneath them.

The RFC recommends a tree that is as flat as possible. Names stay short and look like paper mail addresses, and the design assumes people will search with strings rather than browse down the tree. A maximum of two levels of organisational unit should suffice even for large organisations, and organisations with only a few tens or hundreds of employees should strongly consider using none.

Renaming a department changes the distinguished name of everything beneath it, and references such as aliases, seeAlso, secretary and roleOccupant are one-way and are not updated automatically. So the aim is to minimise changes to the tree. Each organisation should also have Postmaster and Directory Manager entries, plus Secretary entries, using the organizationalRole object class.
sections.eli5: Think of a family tree for names. The guide says to keep it short and wide instead of tall and skinny, so it is quick to find the person you want.

sections.title: Multi-National Organisations
sections.content:
The standard allows only international organisations directly under the root, so a multi-national company must appear as separate entries beneath country or locality entries. The RFC argues the standard should be followed anyway and offers three approaches.

  • Single entity: all entries live in one sub-tree, with alias entries under every country where the organisation operates. This gives a unique view of the organisation but can lead to unnatural names.
  • Loose confederation: each country has its own organisation entry, bound together by aliases for localities and organisational units, which allows several views of the organisation.
  • Loosely linked sub-trees: no aliases at all, only an attribute such as seeAlso. A unified view works only if user interfaces choose to follow the links.

All three can provide an internal directory. In the first two, links are followed by the protocol itself, so organisation-wide searches can be a single X.500 operation.
sections.eli5: A company with offices in many countries can keep one big file and point to it from every country, give each country its own file, or just leave notes saying where to look. Each way has good and bad points.

sections.title: Naming Style
sections.content:
Names should first be unique, and second make querying easy. Reflecting an organisation chart perfectly matters less than that.

An organisation's relative distinguished name (RDN) should usually be its full name, not initials. The RFC prefers University College London over UCL, because acronyms such as AA or CS collide with many other meanings. The short forms belong in the directory as alternative values of the naming attribute, for example UCL as an extra organizationName.

For people, the RDN should be the most common form of the name, such as Steve Kille, with Stephen E. Kille kept as an alternative commonName. The RFC deprecates Lastname Firstname and says to fix the user interface rather than distort the data. Clashing names can be made unique with multi-component RDNs, using extra attributes such as personalTitle, roomNumber, telephoneNumber or userId, instead of artificial values like John Smith 1. Where a country has national naming guidelines, they should generally be followed.
sections.eli5: Write names out in full so nobody mixes them up, like 'University College London' instead of 'UCL'. Keep the short nicknames as extra labels so people can still find you by them.

sections.title: Attribute Values and Languages
sections.content:
Attribute values should be used as the standards document them. Distinguished names should not contain T.61 (Teletex) strings, because most users could not view or type them. Only characters from the printable string syntax should be used in an RDN, and the correct form of the name should be added as an extra value for searches.

The standard of the day had no language support, so the RFC suggests multi-valued attributes holding the local-language value and an English one, for attributes such as friendlyCountryName, localityName and organizationName. When a value needs characters outside PrintableString, supply both a T.61 string and a transliterated PrintableString. The drawback is redundant information, because interfaces cannot tell which language each value is in.

The object class and naming attributes of an entry should be publicly readable unless the entry is meant to be private, since interfaces rely on them to search. The RFC then lists selected attributes with advice and examples, including postalAddress (up to 6 lines of 30 characters each), telephoneNumber in international notation and rfc822mailbox. It also notes that national privacy laws may restrict some attributes.
sections.eli5: Letters like the ones with accents are hard for some computers, so the guide says to also write a plain version. That way everyone can read and search for the name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not substantially discussed in the memo. The one related remark is in the attribute list: a userPassword attribute should not be the same as any system password unless it is certain nobody can read it, and the RFC notes that this was mostly not guaranteed in current implementations.
sections.eli5: The guide barely talks about safety. It only warns not to reuse your real computer password in the phone book, because others might be able to read it.
